Minimal Change Disease

Overview

  • One of the primary glomerular diseases that lead to nephrotic syndrome
  • MCD is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, it accounts for 90% of nephrotic syndrome cases in children younger than 5y and 50% of nephrotic syndrome cases in children older than 10y
  • MCD accounts for 10-15% of nephrotic syndrome cases in adults
  • Minimal change disease has good prognosis

Causes

  • Primary: Idiopathic
  • Secondary
  • Drugs: NSAIDs, antimicrobials, lithium
  • Neoplasms: Hodgkin’s and NHL, leukemia, thymoma
  • Allergy: atopy, vaccinations, insect stings, foods
  • Viral infections (URTI)
  • Primary disease might relapse after exposure to the secondary causes

Pathogenesis

  • Immune attack initiated by T cells against the podocytes for unknown reason
  • T cells injuries the podocyte foot processes leading to effacement of these foot processes and subsequently nephrotic syndrome

Renal biopsy

  • Normal light microscopy, that is why it is called minimal change disease
  • Normal immunofluorescence
  • Effacement of foot processes, microvilli and vacuolations on electron microscopy

Presentation

  • Frothy urine
  • Edema is the first sign, pitting and worse in lower extremities, periorbital edema
  • Abdominal pain due to ascites, severe hypovolemia, peritonitis, pancreatitis, thrombosis, or steroid induced gastritis
  • Hypertension
  • Patients may develop white nails sometimes in bands (Muehrcke's lines) during relapses
  • Adults may develop xanthomas and xanthelasma because of hyperlipidemia

Diagnosis

  • Nephrotic range proteinuria, urine dipstick test 3+, 4+
  • 24 hours urine protein is > 3.5g
  • Urine protein creatinine ratio of more than 3
  • Comprehensive metabolic panel looking for Hypoalbuminemia: serum albumin < 3
  • Renal function test: BUN and creatinine looking for renal dysfunction
  • Serum electrolytes looking for calcium and other electrolytes changes because Total serum calcium and vitamin D decreased due to decrease protein bound calcium and decrease vitamin D binding proteins lost in urine respectively, ionized calcium is usually normal
  • Mild hyponatremia during relapses
  • Elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels and thrombocytosis are usually found in MCD patients during relapse as result of plasma volume contraction
  • Confirmatory test is renal biopsy

Treatment

  • Children younger than 10 presenting with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome: biopsy is not indicated, you treat them like they have minimal change disease
  • Children younger than 10 presenting with features does not go with minimal change disease like gross hematuria, renal dysfunction then renal biopsy is indicated
  • Children older than 10 and Adults: renal biopsy is indicated to establish diagnosis
  • Curative therapy
  • MCD responds very well to corticosteroids
  • Corticosteroids are used in high doses for 12-16 weeks then tapered over 6 months
  • Curative therapy
  • Cyclosporine for steroid resistant patients
  • Cyclophosphamide, Mycophenolate mofetil or rituximab for steroid dependent patients (relapse if steroids are stopped)
  • Supportive therapy
  • Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs
  • Hyperlipidemia treated with statins
  • Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics
  • Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation
  • Infections treated with antibiotics
